title: Reserve Bank governor warns world facing increased supply shocks
full_text:
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock says the world has become more shock-prone in recent years, with the latest spike in oil prices another complication for monetary policy.
She said the recurring shocks had been occurring against a backdrop of persistently weak productivity growth in Australia, which had been weighing on real incomes and wages for years already.
She warned, with continued weak productivity growth, that Australia's economy would not be capable of growing strongly without putting upward pressure on inflation, and that would limit the choices of policymakers in the coming years.
"This is the fundamental challenge for the Australian economy over the next few years," she warned.
"When the growth of potential supply is constrained, inflation is higher for any given level of demand, sharpening the trade-off between our dual objectives of price stability and full employment.
"In a more uncertain and shock-prone world, navigating those trade-offs has become more challenging for central banks."
Ms Bullock said one thing monetary policy could not do was address Australia's slow productivity growth, and while the problem persisted, workers would probably keep experiencing limited growth in real wages.
But she said if inflation kept rising from here, the RBA's Monetary Policy Board would be prepared to lift interest rates even higher, if it was necessary to achieve its inflation mandate.
She made her comments in her speech to the Anika Foundation in Sydney on Tuesday. The title of her speech was Monetary Policy in an Era of Shocks.
Bullock says economy more resilient than in past
Ms Bullock's speech was broadly about the similarities and differences between the oil shocks of the 1970s and today's recurring waves of supply shocks.
She said thankfully, even though the world had been more shock-prone in recent years, Australia's economy was more resilient than it was in the past, for a few reasons.
She said the adoption of a credible inflation target by the RBA in the 1990s had played a "key role" in Australia's improved resilience.
Another key difference, she said, was that Australia's economy had become less dependent on oil than it was in the 1970s.
"This means a given increase in oil prices has a less direct and less pervasive effect on inflation today than it would have in the 1970s," she said.
"[But] this doesn't mean we're immune from adverse supply shocks. They can constrain growth, reduce real incomes and add to inflationary pressures.
"In this environment, our job is to keep inflation expectations anchored and make sure that shocks don't lead to lasting increases in inflation. With inflation and capacity pressures already elevated, recent shocks have added further to the inflation impulse.
"That is why we tightened monetary policy earlier this year and why we remain focused on returning inflation sustainably to target."
Ms Bullock said five months have passed since the United States and Israel began bombing Iran, and since the outbreak of the conflict oil prices have been highly volatile and, as recent days and weeks have demonstrated, conditions can change quickly.
"While the effect on fuel prices and headline inflation has so far been smaller than initially feared, headline inflation remained well above target at 4 per cent in May," she said.
Housing market weaker than expected, more unemployment needed
Staying with the Middle East conflict, she said business confidence in Australia fell sharply at the start of the conflict but has "rebounded somewhat" over recent months.
Ms Bullock said the decline in business conditions and capacity utilisation had been less pronounced, while business investment had been stronger than expected, largely driven by investment in data centres.
But she said Australia's housing market had been a little weaker than expected in recent months.
"We had expected conditions to ease in response to the changed outlook for monetary policy and the rise in the cash rate earlier this year," she said.
"But the housing market has eased by more than we had anticipated in May.
"This appears to reflect a range of factors, including recent policy developments affecting the housing market, and a general softening in housing market sentiment.
"Even so, the easing in established housing prices has so far been modest, following a period of strong growth.
"Price declines have been concentrated in the Sydney and Melbourne markets, but prices in these markets remain around where they were before interest rates started to rise in February this year.
"Furthermore, the most recent data suggest that, notwithstanding the price falls, negative equity remains very limited, affecting less than 1 per cent of borrowers."
Ms Bullock said while the RBA expected property prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary policy did not target housing prices.
"Rather, what matters for monetary policy is how changes in housing prices affect household spending, investment decisions, and, ultimately, inflation," she said.
She said the labour market had also "eased" a bit more than expected in recent months, with the unemployment rate rising a little faster than expected.
But even still, she said, the labour market probably needed more unemployment or underemployment to bring inflation back down.
"Overall, we continue to assess that some further easing in labour market conditions will likely be required to bring inflation back to target," she said.
The national unemployment rate is currently 4.4 per cent. The RBA is forecasting the unemployment rate to be 4.6 per cent by the end of next year.
